label: thm:ImZ-limit-kernel
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ImZ-limit-kernel}
Let \(T>e\), put \(L=\log T\), and let \(t\asymp T\).  Define
\[
A_\infty(z)
:=
2\int_0^1(1-u)\sin(uz)\,du
=
\frac{2(z-\sin z)}{z^2},
\qquad A_\infty(0)=0.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\Re\sum_{\rho}
A_\infty\!\left(
-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)
\right)
+
O\!\left(\frac1L\right),
}
\]
where the sum is over the non-trivial zeros of \(\zeta\), counted with
multiplicity and taken symmetrically.

In particular, under the Riemann Hypothesis this reduces to
\[
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\sum_{\gamma}
A_\infty\!\bigl((\gamma-t)L\bigr)
+
O\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
head: environment
name: Imaginary-part kernel identity

title: Remark
body_md:
The kernel \(A_\infty\) is the odd companion of the Fej\'er kernel appearing
in the real-part identity. Indeed,
\[
\left(\frac{\sin(z/2)}{z/2}\right)^2
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)\cos(uz)\,du,
\]
whereas
\[
A_\infty(z)
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)\sin(uz)\,du.
\]
Thus the real- and imaginary-part kernels arise respectively as the cosine
and sine transforms of the same triangular weight. In particular,
\(A_\infty\) is odd, which explains why its unshifted average over pairs of
zeros exhibits cancellation.
head: environment

label: cor:shifted-imaginary
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Shifted average at the zeros

title: Remark
body_md:
For \(d=0\), the average in the corollary vanishes because \(A_\infty\) is odd.
A microscopic shift therefore reveals information that is invisible when one
evaluates the imaginary part exactly at the zeros. As already observed in
\cite{Ary20HigherMoments}, the main term reaches its maximum at approximately
\[
d=0.4147.
\]

This is interesting in comparison with the real-part identity. The
corresponding average of \(\mathcal C\) is largest at \(d=0\), whereas for the
imaginary part the maximum occurs at a non-zero microscopic shift. Thus the
real and imaginary parts appear to probe the local zero configuration in
genuinely different ways.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Now let \(s\) denote the number of zeros that are simple and on the critical
line. These \(s\) zeros can contribute at most \(s\) positive directions.

The remaining
\[
N(T)-s
\]
zeros are either multiple zeros on the critical line or zeros away from the
critical line. By Main facts \textbf{\#1} and \textbf{\#2}, every two such zeros can contribute
at most one positive direction. Therefore
\[
n_+(G)
\leq
s+\frac{N(T)-s}{2}
=
\frac{N(T)+s}{2}.
\]

Combining this with
\[
n_+(G)
\geq
\left(\frac34-o(1)\right)N(T),
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac{N(T)+s}{2}
\geq
\left(\frac34-o(1)\right)N(T),
\]
and hence\footnote{A very interesting detail of the Anthropic breakthrough is that one of Claude's sub-agents first arrived at an unconditional \(1/2\) bound using essentially the direction-counting argument described here. The orchestrating agent noted that this would already improve the previous \(5/12\approx41.7\%\) record, but initially regarded the claim with considerable suspicion and sent several other agents to referee it. The following morning, a new sub-agent was explicitly tasked with pushing the \(1/2\) argument further; this led to the stronger \(2/3\) argument used in the final proof.
}
\[
\boxed{
s
\geq
\left(\frac12-o(1)\right)N(T).
}
\]

Thus this elementary direction-counting argument already shows that at least
half of the zeros are simple and lie on the critical line.
head: manual
name: $\%50$ of zeros are on the critical line

label: lem:recursion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:recursion}
For every \(k\geq1\),
\[
\Im_k(t)-\Im_{k+1}(t)
=
\frac{1}{L}\mathcal C_k'(t).
\]
Consequently, for every integer \(M\geq1\),
\[
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\frac1L\sum_{k=1}^M\mathcal C_k'(t)
+
\Im_{M+1}(t).
\]
Moreover, for \(M=\lceil L\rceil\), then
\[
\Im_{M+1}(t)\ll \frac1L .
\]
head: environment
name: Recursive identity

label: lem:Ck-zero
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Ck-zero}
Let \(T>e\), \(L=\log T\), and \(t\asymp T\). Then, for every integer
\(k\geq1\),
\[
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-1+
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\widetilde S_k\!\left(
-\frac{iL}{2}
\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)
\right)
+
O_k\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
Writing \(\rho=\beta+i\gamma\), this is
\[
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-1+
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\widetilde S_k\!\left(
\frac{L}{2}
\left(
(\gamma-t)-i\left(\beta-\frac12\right)
\right)
\right)
+
O_k\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
More precisely, for \(1\leq k\leq 2L\), the error term may be
written as \(E_k(t)\), where
\[
E_k(t)\ll \frac1L,
\qquad
E_k'(t)\ll \frac1{TL},
\]
uniformly for \(t\asymp T\).
head: environment
name: Higher-order Fej\'er identity

label: lem:odd-tail
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:odd-tail}
For an integer \(M\geq1\), put
\[
B_M(z):=A_\infty(z)-A_M(z)
=2\int_0^1(1-u)^{M+1}\sin(uz)\,du.
\]
Then, uniformly for \(t\asymp T\),
\[
\Re\sum_\rho
B_M\!\left(-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)\right)
=
\Im_{M+1}(t)+O\!\left(\frac1L\right),
\]
where the zero sum is taken symmetrically.  In particular, if
\(M\geq(1/2+\varepsilon)L\), then the left-hand side is
\(O_\varepsilon(L^{-1})\).
head: environment
name: Odd-kernel tail identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
\[
z_\rho(t)
:=
-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:recursion},
\[
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\frac1L\sum_{k=1}^{M}\mathcal C_k'(t)
+
\Im_{M+1}(t).
\]
Choose \(M\asymp L\).  Then
\[
\Im_{M+1}(t)\ll \frac1L.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-zero},
\[
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-1+
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\widetilde S_k\!\left(\frac{z_\rho(t)}2\right)
+
E_k(t),
\]
where
\[
E_k'(t)\ll \frac1{TL}
\]
uniformly for \(1\leq k\leq M\).
Since
\[
z_\rho'(t)=-L,
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac1L\mathcal C_k'(t)
=
-\frac12
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\widetilde S_k'\!\left(\frac{z_\rho(t)}2\right)
+
\frac1L E_k'(t).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac1L\sum_{k=1}^{M}\mathcal C_k'(t)
=
\Re\sum_{\rho}A_M\bigl(z_\rho(t)\bigr)
+
O\!\left(\frac1{TL}\right),
\]
where
\[
A_M(z)
:=
-\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{M}
\widetilde S_k'\!\left(\frac z2\right).
\]

Using
\[
\widetilde S_k\!\left(\frac z2\right)
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)^k\cos(uz)\,du,
\]
we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_M(z)
&=
2\int_0^1
u\sum_{k=1}^{M}(1-u)^k\sin(uz)\,du\\
&=
2\int_0^1
(1-u)\bigl(1-(1-u)^M\bigr)\sin(uz)\,du.
\end{aligned}
\]
It remains to replace \(A_M\) by \(A_\infty\).  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:odd-tail},
\[
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\bigl(A_\infty-A_M\bigr)
\!\left(-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)\right)
=O\!\left(\frac1L\right)
\]
for our choice \(M\asymp L\).  Hence
\[
\Re\sum_{\rho}
A_M\!\left(-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)\right)
=
\Re\sum_{\rho}
A_\infty\!\left(-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)\right)
+O\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]

Consequently,
\[
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\Re\sum_{\rho}
A_\infty\!\left(
-iL\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)
\right)
+
O\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
This is unconditional.  If the Riemann Hypothesis is assumed, then
\(\rho=\frac12+i\gamma\), and the identity reduces to
\[
\Im Z\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\sum_{\gamma}
A_\infty\!\big((\gamma-t)L\big)
+
O\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Differentiating \(\mathcal C_k(t)\), we obtain
\[
\frac1L\mathcal C_k'(t)
=
\frac{2}{L}\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\frac{\log n}{L}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k
\sin(t\log n).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Im_k(t)-\Im_{k+1}(t)
&=
\frac{2}{L}\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\left[
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k
-
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^{k+1}
\right]
\sin(t\log n)\\
&=
\frac{2}{L}\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\frac{\log n}{L}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k
\sin(t\log n),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves
\[
\Im_k(t)-\Im_{k+1}(t)=\frac1L\mathcal C_k'(t).
\]
Summing over \(1\leq k\leq M\) gives the telescoping identity.

Finally,
\[
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^{M+1}
\leq
n^{-(M+1)/L},
\]
and hence, if \(M\geq(1/2+\varepsilon)L\),
\[
|\Im_{M+1}(t)|
\leq
\frac2L
\sum_{n\geq2}
\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^{1+\varepsilon}}
\ll_\varepsilon\frac1L.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(s_0=\frac12+it\) and introduce the odd entire transform
\[
H_M(w):=L B_M(-iLw)
=-2iL\int_0^1(1-u)^{M+1}\sinh(Luw)\,du.
\]
Apply to \(H_M(s-s_0)\) the same two-line contour argument used in
Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-zero}.  On the line \(\Re s>1\), expanding
\(\zeta'/\zeta\) into its Dirichlet series and writing the hyperbolic
sine as a difference of exponentials gives the prime polynomial with
weight \((1-\log n/L)^{M+1}\).  Reflecting the left-hand line by the
functional equation gives its complex conjugate.  Taking the real part
of the residue identity therefore yields
\[
\Re\sum_\rho B_M\!\left(-iL(\rho-s_0)\right)
=
\frac{2}{L}\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^{M+1}
\sin(t\log n)
+O\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
The sum on the right is precisely \(\Im_{M+1}(t)\).  The pole and
Gamma-factor terms are \(O(L^{-1})\), by the same Stirling estimates as
in Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-zero}.  Finally, if
\(M\geq(1/2+\varepsilon)L\), Lemma~\ref{lem:recursion} gives
\(\Im_{M+1}(t)\ll_\varepsilon L^{-1}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is a higher-order extension of the unconditional Fej\'er-kernel
identity proved by the author in \cite{Ary22}, corresponding to the case
\(k=1\).  Under the Riemann Hypothesis, the \(k=1\) identity was proved
earlier by Gonek \cite{Gonek}. \\

We briefly describe the architecture of the argument.  We begin with a
contour on the right of the critical strip, where the logarithmic derivative
of the zeta function can be expanded as an absolutely convergent Dirichlet
series.  We then move the contour to the left of the critical strip.  The
difference between the two contour integrals is given by the residues of the
non-trivial zeros, together with the contribution of the pole of the zeta
function.  On the left-hand contour we use the functional equation for the
logarithmic derivative to reflect the zeta term back to the right-hand
half-plane, where it can once again be expanded into a Dirichlet series.
The remaining term arising from the functional equation is the Gamma-factor
contribution.  This is treated separately by Stirling's formula, exactly as
in the \(k=1\) argument.  In this way no assumption on the location of the
non-trivial zeros is required.\\

Put
\[
s_0:=\frac12+it
\]
and, for \(k\geq1\), define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Gk-def}
G_k(w)
:=
L\int_{-1}^{1}(1-|u|)^k e^{Luw}\,du.
\end{equation}
The function \(G_k\) is entire and even.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Gk-Sk-complex}
\frac1L G_k(w)
=
\widetilde S_k\!\left(-\frac{iLw}{2}\right).
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\[
\frac1L G_k(w)
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)^k\cosh(Luw)\,du
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)^k
\cos\!\left(-iLuw\right)\,du.
\]

Let \(c=1+\delta\), where \(0<\delta<1\), and consider
\[
I_k^{+}(t)
:=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(c)}
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)
G_k(s-s_0)\,ds.
\]
Since \(c>1\), we may use the absolutely convergent expansion
\[
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)
=
-\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s}.
\]
For \(n>1\), Perron's formula gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Gk-Perron}
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(c)}
n^{-s}G_k(s-s_0)\,ds
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
n^{-s_0}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k,
& n<T,\\[3mm]
0,&n>T.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Iplus}
I_k^{+}(t)
=
-\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^{s_0}}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k.
\end{equation}
If we write
\[
P_k(t)
:=
\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^{s_0}}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Ck-P}
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-\frac{2}{L}\Re P_k(t),
\qquad
I_k^{+}(t)=-P_k(t).
\end{equation}

We next introduce the corresponding integral on the line
\(\Re s=1-c=-\delta\):
\[
I_k^{-}(t)
:=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(1-c)}
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)
G_k(s-s_0)\,ds.
\]
By the residue theorem, the difference between the two contour
integrals is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:residue-strip}
I_k^{+}(t)-I_k^{-}(t)
=
\sum_{\rho}G_k(\rho-s_0)
-
G_k(1-s_0).
\end{equation}
Here the sum is over all non-trivial zeros of \(\zeta\), counted with
multiplicity.  The second term comes from the pole of \(\zeta\) at
\(s=1\), whose residue in \(\zeta'/\zeta\) is \(-1\).
Since \(0<\delta<1\), no trivial zero lies between the two vertical
lines. \\

We now treat \(I_k^{-}(t)\) by the functional equation.  Using
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:FE-logder}
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(s)
=
\frac{\chi'}{\chi}(s)
-
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(1-s),
\end{equation}
we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Iminus-FE}
I_k^{-}(t)
=
\Gamma_k(t)-J_k(t),
\end{equation}
where
\[
\Gamma_k(t)
:=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(1-c)}
\frac{\chi'}{\chi}(s)
G_k(s-s_0)\,ds
\]
and
\[
J_k(t)
:=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(1-c)}
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(1-s)
G_k(s-s_0)\,ds.
\]

In \(J_k(t)\), make the change of variables \(z=1-s\).  Since \(G_k\)
is even and
\[
1-s_0=\frac12-it=\overline{s_0},
\]
we obtain
\[
J_k(t)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi i}
\int_{(c)}
\frac{\zeta'}{\zeta}(z)
G_k(z-\overline{s_0})\,dz.
\]
We may again expand \(\zeta'/\zeta\) into its Dirichlet series, and the
same calculation as in \eqref{eq:Gk-Perron} gives
\[
J_k(t)
=
-\sum_{n<T}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^{\overline{s_0}}}
\left(1-\frac{\log n}{L}\right)^k
=
-\overline{P_k(t)}.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Iminus-final}
I_k^{-}(t)
=
\Gamma_k(t)+\overline{P_k(t)}.
\end{equation}

Substituting \eqref{eq:Iplus} and \eqref{eq:Iminus-final} into
\eqref{eq:residue-strip}, we find
\[
-P_k(t)-\overline{P_k(t)}-\Gamma_k(t)
=
\sum_{\rho}G_k(\rho-s_0)-G_k(1-s_0).
\]
Taking real parts,
\[
-2\Re P_k(t)
=
\Re\sum_{\rho}G_k(\rho-s_0)
-
\Re G_k(1-s_0)
+
\Re\Gamma_k(t).
\]
Therefore, by \eqref{eq:Ck-P},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Ck-pre-gamma}
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
\frac1L
\Re\sum_{\rho}G_k(\rho-s_0)
-
\frac1L\Re G_k(1-s_0)
+
\frac1L\Re\Gamma_k(t).
\end{equation}

It remains to evaluate the Gamma-factor contribution.  As in the proof
of the corresponding lemmas in the Landau--Gonek formula, we move the
line in \(\Gamma_k(t)\) from \(\Re s=1-c\) to \(\Re s=1/2\).  The
possible contribution from the singularity at \(s=0\) is negligible for
\(t\asymp T\).  Hence
\[
\Gamma_k(t)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\frac{\chi'}{\chi}\left(\frac12+i\tau\right)
G_k\bigl(i(\tau-t)\bigr)\,d\tau
+
O_k(T^{-1}).
\]
Using
\[
G_k(iv)
=
L\widetilde S_k\left(\frac{Lv}{2}\right)
\]
and making the change of variables
\[
x=\frac{L(\tau-t)}2,
\]
we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Gamma-Sk}
\Gamma_k(t)
=
\frac1\pi
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\widetilde S_k(x)
\frac{\chi'}{\chi}
\left(
\frac12+i\left(t+\frac{2x}{L}\right)
\right)\,dx
+
O_k(T^{-1}).
\end{equation}

On the critical line, For \(|y|\geq2\), Stirling's formula gives
\[
\frac{\chi'}{\chi}\left(\frac12+iy\right)
=
-\log\frac{|y|}{2\pi}
+
O\left(\frac{1}{1+y^2}\right).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\widetilde S_k(x)\,dx=\pi,
\]
while
\[
\widetilde S_k(x)\ll_k \frac{1}{1+x^2}.
\]
It follows from \eqref{eq:Gamma-Sk}, uniformly for \(t\asymp T\), that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Gamma-main}
\Gamma_k(t)
=
-\log\frac{t}{2\pi}+O_k(1).
\end{equation}
Moreover, these estimates may be made uniform for
\(1\leq k\leq 2L\).  For real \(x\),
\[
0\leq \widetilde S_k(x)
\ll
\min\left\{\frac{1}{k+1},\frac{k}{1+x^2}\right\},
\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}\widetilde S_k(x)\,dx=\pi.
\]
Repeating the preceding argument after differentiation with respect to
\(t\), and using Stirling's formula once more, gives
\[
\Gamma_k'(t)\ll \frac1T
\]
uniformly for \(1\leq k\leq 2L\) and \(t\asymp T\).  Similarly, from
\eqref{eq:Gk-def}, by integration by parts,
\[
G_k(1-s_0)=O(1),
\qquad
\frac{d}{dt}G_k(1-s_0)\ll\frac1T,
\]
uniformly in the same range.

Now define
\[
E_k(t)
:=
1-\frac1L\Re G_k(1-s_0)
+\frac1L\Re\Gamma_k(t).
\]
Since
\[
\Gamma_k(t)
=
-\log\frac{t}{2\pi}+O(1)
\]
uniformly in this range, and \(t\asymp T\), we have
\[
E_k(t)\ll\frac1L,
\qquad
E_k'(t)\ll\frac1{TL}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:Ck-pre-gamma} becomes
\[
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-1+
\frac1L\Re\sum_{\rho}G_k(\rho-s_0)
+
E_k(t).
\]
Finally, by \eqref{eq:Gk-Sk-complex},
\[
\frac1L G_k(\rho-s_0)
=
\widetilde S_k\left(
-\frac{iL}{2}(\rho-s_0)
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathcal C_k(t)
=
-1+
\Re\sum_{\rho}
\widetilde S_k\left(
-\frac{iL}{2}
\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)
\right)
+
E_k(t),
\]
where
\[
E_k(t)\ll\frac1L,
\qquad
E_k'(t)\ll\frac1{TL}.
\]
This proves the lemma.
head: environment

label: prop:short-imaginary
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:short-imaginary}
Let \(0<\alpha\leq1\) be fixed and \(t\asymp T\). Then
\[
\Im Z_\alpha\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\Re\sum_\rho
A_\infty\!\left(
-iL_\alpha
\left(\rho-\frac12-it\right)
\right)
+
O_\alpha\!\left(\frac1L\right),
\]
where
\[
A_\infty(z)
=
2\int_0^1(1-u)\sin(uz)\,du
=
\frac{2(z-\sin z)}{z^2}.
\]
The sum over the non-trivial zeros is understood symmetrically.

In particular, under the Riemann Hypothesis,
\[
\Im Z_\alpha\!\left(\frac12+it\right)
=
\sum_\gamma
A_\infty\!\left(
\alpha L(\gamma-t)
\right)
+
O_\alpha\!\left(\frac1L\right).
\]
head: environment
name: Short-truncation imaginary identity

title: Proof
body_md: The proof is the same as that of the full-length identity, with replaced throughout by $\alpha L.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(L=\log T\). From the definition of \(\Im_\beta\),
\[
\Im_\beta(t)
=
\frac{2}{\beta L}
\sum_{n<T^\beta}
\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\left(
1-\frac{\log n}{\beta L}
\right)
\sin(t\log n).
\]
By the Landau--Gonek formula,
\[
\frac1{N(T)}
\sum_{0<\gamma<T}n^{i\gamma}
\sim
-\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n\,L}
\]
in the range \(n<T^\beta\). Hence the shift by
\(-2\pi d/L\) gives
\[
\frac{1}{N(T)}
\sum_{0<\gamma<T}
\Im_\beta\!\left(
\gamma-\frac{2\pi d}{L}
\right)
\sim
\frac{2}{\beta L^2}
\sum_{n<T^\beta}
\frac{\Lambda(n)^2}{n}
\left(
1-\frac{\log n}{\beta L}
\right)
\sin\!\left(
2\pi d\frac{\log n}{L}
\right).
\]
Using
\[
\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)^2\sim x\log x
\]
and partial summation, with
\[
u=\frac{\log n}{L},
\]
the last expression tends to
\[
\frac{2}{\beta}
\int_0^\beta
u\left(1-\frac{u}{\beta}\right)
\sin(2\pi du)\,du.
\]
The closed form follows by an elementary integration.
